name: Cold Cream (Cetaphil/Cold cream)

lead: Cold cream is a thick cream used to smooth skin and remove makeup. It is a water-in-oil emulsion, with water dispersed in a larger amount of oil, which is what leaves skin soft after cleansing; the name refers to the cooling feel it leaves.[1]

For looks, it gives a gentle way to remove makeup and sunscreen and to moisturise dry skin, supporting a smoother, less irritated complexion. Brands include Pond's and Noxzema, and the Cetaphil moisturising line has been studied in eczema and rosacea.[1][3][4]

paras: Users massage a layer onto dry skin, then wipe or rinse it off. It is also used as a facial mask, lip balm, shaving cream and moisturiser.[1]

Case reports describe allergic contact dermatitis from moisturisers, and comparison studies show topical products differ in how irritating they are.[5][6] Oily formulas may feel heavy on very oily or acne-prone skin.

chain: Massage cold cream over skin and makeup
Oil phase lifts makeup and leaves moisture
Clean, soft skin without harsh stripping
angle.text: Cold cream cleans and moisturises in one step. Users apply it to remove makeup and as a rich night moisturiser.

lead: Cold cream (ceratum refrigerans) is a facial cream used to smooth skin and remove makeup. It is a water-in-oil emulsion, unlike vanishing cream which is oil-in-water, and the name refers to the cooling sensation it leaves on skin [1].

For looks, it works as a one-step cleanser and moisturiser. The oil phase dissolves makeup and sunscreen when massaged over the face, and wiping or rinsing it off leaves skin soft, which supports a smoother, less dry-looking complexion without the tight feel some foaming cleansers leave. Beyond cleansing, it is used as a mask, lip balm, shaving cream and rich night moisturiser [1].

Traditional versions used beeswax, plant oils, rose water and scent; modern ones usually replace plant oils with mineral oil and add glycerin, lanolin or alcohol [1]. The physician Galen in second-century Greece is credited with inventing it, and variations have been used for nearly 2,000 years, with borax later added to stabilise the beeswax emulsion [1][2]. In the twentieth century Pond's made cold cream a mass-market staple, promoting it from the 1910s alongside its vanishing cream [3].

The wiki entry also covers Cetaphil, a separate skincare brand developed in Texas in 1947 whose cleansers and moisturising creams are commonly mentioned in the same skincare routines and have been examined in clinical trials [4][5][6].
infobox: Pond's, Noxzema [1]; Cetaphil is a separate line [6]
Makeup removal, moisturiser, mask, lip balm, shaving cream [1]
Developed in 1947 in Texas; now owned by Galderma [6]

paras: Cold cream is a semisolid emulsion. Water-in-oil structure means the oil is the continuous phase, which gives a protective, occlusive feel and thicker texture than a lotion [1][2]. Wikipedia lists its main uses as moisturising and skin treatment, including facial masks and lip balm, and also shaving cream and makeup remover [1]. Jojoba oil became common from the 1970s as a substitute for spermaceti, a whale-derived wax [1].

Beeswax was the original emulsifier but worked poorly and could separate, so small amounts of borax were added; the borax reacts with fatty acids in the wax to form a soap that stabilises the cream [1]. Plant oils spoil quickly when mixed with water, so cold cream was historically made in small batches at home or in the pharmacy [1]. Most modern versions replace plant oils with mineral oil and add alcohol, glycerin and lanolin [1]. In France it is still called cerat de Galien, Galen's wax [1].

Galen of second-century Greece is credited with creating it, with a formula of rosewater, beeswax and almond or olive oil [1]. A 1650 London Dispensatory formula by Nicholas Culpeper, an 1814 poem and an 1857 account all describe versions, and the 1857 account by George Piesse notes the modern formula differed in scent and quality from Galen's but was still essentially grease and water; it lists scents such as camphor, almond, violet and rose [1]. A 1920 household encyclopedia listed uses including softening and cooling skin after sunburn and cleansing [1].

Pond's began in 1846 when Utica, New York pharmacist Theron T. Pond created a witch hazel extract sold as a patent medicine; the company was formed between 1849 and 1852 and Pond died in 1852. It was incorporated as Pond's Extract Company in 1914 [3]. From the 1910s the brand moved toward cosmetics, led by Vanishing Cream and Cold Cream, which by 1914 were promoted together with the line Every normal skin needs these two creams [3]. In the 1920s the company used testimonials from royalty and politicians, including Queen Marie of Romania, and advertised in magazines such as Vogue. Pond's merged with Chesebrough Manufacturing Company in 1955, Unilever acquired Chesebrough-Ponds in 1987, and Unilever spun Pond's into a standalone business, Elida Beauty, in 2021; the page lists Evermark as current owner. Its largest markets are reported to include Spain and parts of Asia such as India, Japan and Thailand [3]. Noxzema is the other widely sold US cold-cream brand named by Wikipedia [1].

Cetaphil was developed in 1947 in Texas and is headquartered in Fort Worth; Galderma is the current parent and Nestle a former one. The line includes cleansers, bar soap, cream, lotion and moisturisers sold in grocery stores and pharmacies in the United States, Canada, India and Nepal, and in pharmacies in about 100 other countries [6]. Before 2021 the cleanser's listed ingredients included water, cetyl alcohol, propylene glycol, sodium lauryl sulfate, stearyl alcohol and three parabens; in 2021 the formula changed to add niacinamide, panthenol and glycerin [6]. Cetaphil is not described as a cold cream in these sources; it appears in this entry because its cleansers and moisturising creams are used for similar gentle cleansing and moisturising and have been trialled in skin conditions [4][5].

Users massage a layer of cold cream onto dry skin and wipe or rinse it off, which dissolves makeup and sunscreen while leaving moisture behind. It is used on lips, as a mask and as a shaving cream [1]. Oily formulas can feel heavy on very oily or acne-prone skin, and moisturisers can occasionally cause contact allergy [7].
Allergic contact dermatitis has been reported with moisturisers [7]. A comparative study of five commonly used topical products found differences in cutaneous irritation [8].

No studies on cold cream as a cleanser were found. Related trials of Cetaphil products exist: a review of four randomised studies of Cetaphil and Excipial moisturisers in atopic dermatitis rated the evidence very low to moderate quality [4], and a randomised trial examined Cetaphil moisturising cream as part of a daily regimen for rosacea [5].

lore.intro: Cold cream is discussed as an old-fashioned but still-used makeup remover and moisturiser, and Cetaphil as a gentle, widely recommended basic skincare line [1][6].

timeline.event: Galen is credited with the original cold cream, made with rosewater, beeswax and almond or olive oil [1].
Nicholas Culpeper's London Dispensatory gives a cold cream formula with white wax and rose oil [1].
A poem attributed to Dr. Russell credits cold cream with clearing pimples and smoothing wrinkles [1].
Utica pharmacist Theron T. Pond creates a witch hazel extract, the origin of the Pond's company [3].
George Piesse's The Art of Perfumery notes that modern cold cream differs in scent and quality from Galen's but is still essentially grease and water [1].
Pond's is incorporated as Pond's Extract Company and promotes its vanishing and cold creams together [3].
Harmsworth's Household Encyclopedia lists cold cream uses including softening skin and cleansing [1].
Jojoba oil becomes common as a substitute for spermaceti, a whale-derived wax, in cold creams [1].
Unilever acquires Chesebrough-Ponds, expanding the Pond's brand internationally [3].
Cetaphil changes its cleanser formula to add niacinamide, panthenol and glycerin; Unilever spins Pond's into a standalone business [3][6].
